name: Monster Walks on Forefeet
description: A monster walk variation performed on the balls of the feet (tiptoe position) while maintaining a mini band resistance above the knees. Rising onto the forefeet during the lateral walk adds a continuous calf and ankle stability demand to the standard gluteus medius activation of monster walks, creating a combined lower limb rehabilitation stimulus. This variation is used in advanced ankle rehabilitation, calf strengthening, and hip-ankle integration programs.

execution.starting_position: Place a mini band loop above the knees. Rise onto the balls of both feet. Assume a quarter-squat position with hips pushed back slightly, feet hip-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure adequate space for 10-12 lateral steps in each direction. Begin with a lighter band to master the balance before adding resistance.
steps: Step 1: Rise onto the forefeet with the band above the knees and maintain this elevated position throughout.
Step 2: Take a lateral step to the right, keeping the toes forward and the band taut.
Step 3: Bring the left foot partially in (maintaining some width) to keep band tension.
Step 4: Continue walking laterally for the prescribed steps, then reverse direction. The forefeet stay elevated throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously. The sustained tiptoe position is demanding — do not hold the breath.
common_mistakes: Lowering the heels during the walk — the forefoot elevation must be sustained throughout
Letting the feet drift parallel or together, losing band tension
Excessive forward lean — maintain an upright torso
safety_considerations: If ankle stability is compromised, begin with standard monster walks before this elevated variation
Perform near a wall for safety during initial attempts
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lateral step width should maintain band tension without forcing knee valgus. Stay on the forefeet throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1 step per 1-1.5 seconds. Controlled — not rushing.
coaching_cues: Heels never touch the floor — stay on the balls of the feet the whole time
Keep toes pointing forward — not outward
Feel both the outer hip and the calf working simultaneously
